name: Andvaranaut
powers: Cursed to bring death and misfortune to every possessor after the dwarf who made it.
description: Andvaranaut is the ring at the heart of the cursed gold of the dwarf Andvari, taken from him by Loki at the waterfall Gnitaheiðr after the god caught the dwarf in the shape of a pike. When Andvari was forced to give up his treasure hoard, he kept a single ring, and when Loki wrenched that away too, the dwarf laid a curse on the gold: it would destroy every possessor who came after him. The treasure passed to the chieftain Hreiðmarr as wergild for his murdered son Otr, then to the dragon Fáfnir, and finally to the hero Sigurðr, and ruin followed each owner. The story is told in the Völsunga saga and echoed in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied, and Andvaranaut is widely seen as the direct ancestor of the Ring of the Nibelung in Richard Wagner's opera cycle. Its name, 'Andvari's gift', has become shorthand for a treasure that brings only doom.

name: Ægishjálmr
powers: Strikes fear into enemies and grants the wearer protection in battle.
description: Ægishjálmr, the 'helm of awe' or 'helm of terror', is a protective sign of Norse and Icelandic tradition, drawn as a wheel of radiating prongs or staves. In the poem Fáfnismál the dragon Fáfnir is said to have worn the helm of awe, and the hero Sigurðr takes it as part of the dragon's hoard, suggesting a literal helmet in the oldest layer of the story. From the early modern period the name came to be attached to an eight-armed magical stave of the Icelandic galdrabækur, drawn on the forehead between the brows or on the brow of a person to strike fear into enemies and give victory and protection; the 17th-century grimoire tradition is where the familiar branched symbol comes from. The two uses are sometimes confused, and it is likely the modern stave design and the Eddic helmet are different things that share a name. Ægishjálmr remains one of the most reproduced of all Icelandic staves, in tattoos, jewellery, and fantasy art.

name: Amber Jewelry
description: Necklaces, pendants, and beads of Baltic amber, the fossil resin thrown up on Danish shores, worn as adornment and as protection since the Stone Age. Danish Bronze Age graves hold hundreds of amber beads, and amber amulets were believed to guard against the evil eye and sickness, while small amber figures of animals and tools were made for magic and trade. In the Baltic legend the sea-goddess Jurate's palace of amber broke apart, and the pieces scattered across the waves became the amber that still washes up on the beaches. The stone's warmth and light have given it a lasting place in charms for health and luck.
source: Bronze Age graves, Denmark; Baltic amber legend

name: Aegis
powers: Scatters armies with terror; bears the head of Medusa (gorgoneion).
description: The storm-bearing shield of Zeus, lent to Athena and sometimes Apollo, an aegis of goatskin fringed with gold tassels; in Homer it scatters armies with terror and houses the gorgoneion, the severed head of Medusa. Hephaestus forged its golden version for Zeus, and the aegis became Athena's emblem in art, worn over her breast or carried on her arm. It marks divine protection and terror in Greek epic, and the name later passed into ordinary speech for any protecting force or shield of authority. The gorgoneion set on its face remained a common apotropaic image on shields and buildings through antiquity.
source: Homer, Iliad (with the gorgoneion also in Hesiod and later mythographers)

name: Shield of Achilles
material: Bronze, tin, gold, silver with enamelled core
powers: Depicts the whole cosmos: earth, sea, sky, two cities, war, peace, and the encircling Ocean; impenetrable in battle.
description: The great shield Hephaestus forged for Achilles in the Iliad, the poem's supreme example of the god-smith's craft and the model of the cosmic artifact in Greek epic. Five metal layers of bronze, tin, gold and silver carry scenes of the whole world: earth, sea and sky with sun, moon and stars, two cities, one at peace with weddings, lawsuits and dance, one besieged in war, fields ploughed by oxen, a ripe harvest, a vineyard, a cattle raid with lions, and a choir of dancers, all encircled by the stream of Ocean. Homer describes its making at length when Thetis visits Hephaestus, and the finished shield mirrors the mortal world Achilles is about to leave; the passage became the defining example of ekphrasis, a poem describing a work of art. The motif was imitated in the Shield of Heracles and in Virgil's Roman answer, and it remains the archetype of the hero's world-in-miniature, an object whose decoration, not its metal, gives it power.

name: Crown of Ariadne
powers: Set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis after Ariadne's death.
description: The golden crown Ariadne wore when she helped Theseus escape the labyrinth of Crete after he slew the Minotaur, and the circlet Dionysus later set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis. In Catullus' Carmen 64 the crown is the gift that marks Ariadne's fate after Theseus abandons her on Naxos, where Dionysus finds her and raises her crown to heaven in her honour; Apollodorus also preserves the tradition of the celestial setting. Different sources make Hephaestus or Dionysus its maker, and its gems were said to shine with a brightness of their own in the night sky. The seven bright stars of Corona Borealis still carry her name, and the crown is a standing emblem of the abandoned bride turned into a celestial monument. In Renaissance and later art the corona of Ariadne appears again and again, marrying astronomy and myth in a single golden ring of stars.

name: Shield of Aeneas
powers: Shows the future of Rome, from Romulus to the triumph of Augustus at Actium.
description: The shield Vulcan, the Roman Hephaestus, forged for Aeneas at the request of his mother Venus, engraved with the future of Rome and described at length at the close of the eighth book of the Aeneid. Its bronze bears the city's destiny: the she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabine women, Rome's kings, the defence against the Gauls, the punishment of the conspirator Catiline, and the sea battle of Actium with Augustus triumphing over Antony and Cleopatra, all framed within scenes of the empire that was to come. The ekphrasis deliberately answers the Shield of Achilles in Homer: where Achilles' shield shows the whole cosmos and mortal life, Aeneas' shows a single people's ordained future. The shield is the emblem of Roman destiny made visible in metal, and the image of Aeneas lifting onto his shoulder a shield whose glory he does not understand closes the poem's first half. It remains the classic portrait of a nation reading itself in its own artifacts.

name: Ancile
maker: Fell from heaven in the reign of Numa; copies made by the smith Mamurius Veturius
powers: Pledge of Rome's eternity; twelve copies kept the true shield hidden from thieves.
description: The ancile was the sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa Pompilius, Rome's second king, and was kept as a pledge that the city would rule the world as long as the shield was preserved. Fearing theft, Numa had the smith Mamurius Veturius make eleven identical copies, so that the twelve shields carried in procession by the Salian priests could not be told apart, and the legend adds that Mamurius asked as his only reward that his name be sung in the Salian hymn. Plutarch, Ovid in the Fasti, and Servius all tell the story, and the Salii struck the bronze ancilia with staffs as they danced through the city each March at the opening of the campaigning season. The shield thus joined the palladium and the fire of Vesta among the pignora imperii, the tokens of Rome's eternity. Its name passed into later usage as a word for any safeguard of the state.
source: Plutarch, Life of Numa; Ovid, Fasti (Book 3); Servius, on the Aeneid

name: Aegis
powers: Provides impenetrable protection and bears the terrifying visage of Medusa.
description: The aegis, the storm-shield of Zeus, is the awesome goatskin or bronze buckler with which the god of the Iliad terrifies armies and shakes the field of battle, and which his daughter Athena also wears in the fight; its name, from the Greek for 'goat', points to its origin as a ritual skin, though Homer treats it as a wrought shield forged by Hephaestus. Its surface bears the severed head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose gaze turns all who meet it to stone, so that the shield is as much a weapon of terror as a defence. Zeus lends the aegis to his champions and shakes it as a sign of wrath, and in Athena's hands it accompanies the goddess of war and wisdom into battle. In art the aegis appears as a scaly breastplate fringed with serpents, with the gorgoneion at its centre. The word has passed into English for any protective backing or patronage.

name: Ankh
powers: Symbol of life; grants vitality to the bearer.
description: The ankh, the looped cross that is the Egyptian hieroglyph for 'life', is the most recognisable of Egyptian symbols, appearing on temple walls, tomb paintings, and amulets for more than three thousand years. Shaped as a cross with a looped handle, it was carried by gods and goddesses, who hold it to the nostrils of kings and of the dead to breathe life into them, and pharaohs are shown with the ankh as the sign of the eternal life that kingship conferred. It is at once a writing sign, a sacred object, and a talisman: placed on the lips and eyes of mummies, worn as jewellery, and offered to the deceased in the scenes of the Book of the Dead. Through the Coptic Church, whose cross owes its form to the ankh, the sign became the crux ansata of Christian Egypt. It has been adopted in modern culture as a symbol of life and of the African heritage. Its meaning, simply and permanently, is life itself.

name: Sword of Attila
material: Iron with gold and gem-set hilt
powers: Blade of world dominion pledged to Attila.
description: The sword said to have belonged to Attila the Hun is known first from the Roman historian Jordanes, who writes in his Getica that a shepherd found a blade in the ground after cattle had trodden the place bare, and that Attila called it the Sword of Mars, a pledge of world dominion. By the eleventh century a richly decorated sabre was honoured in the Hungarian royal court as the Sword of Attila; the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld records that Queen Anastasia gave it to Otto, Duke of Bavaria, in 1063. The weapon that survives, kept in the imperial treasury of the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna and traditionally called the Sabre of Charlemagne, is in fact a Hungarian sabre of the early tenth century, long after Attila's death, with a gilded, gem-set hilt and curved blade of steppe form. The sword is sometimes said to have been recovered from Charlemagne's grave by Otto III in the year 1000, and to have been carried in the coronations of Holy Roman Emperors. No physical link to Attila can be proven, but the legend made the blade one of Europe's most famous royal relics.

name: Arthur's Mantle
powers: Made the wearer invisible while still allowing them to see everything around them.
description: Arthur's mantle, Llen Arthur, is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain in medieval Welsh tradition. Whoever wore the cloak became invisible, yet could still see everything about him, a power that made it a garment of spies and guardians. The treasure list, which survives in several Welsh manuscripts from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, records the object among the possessions of the old heroes of British legend, and one version places the mantle 'in Cornwall'. The cloak belongs to the Welsh Arthur of marvel and quest, distinct from the later continental king of Malory and the French romances. Its power of selective invisibility, hiding the wearer while leaving his sight intact, is echoed in later folklore and fantasy. Unlike Arthur's sword and ship, the mantle appears nowhere outside the Welsh treasure catalogue, and it remains one of the more mysterious items in the list.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Ardagh Chalice
material: Silver, bronze, gold filigree, glass and enamel
description: The Ardagh Chalice is a two-handled silver cup made in Ireland in the eighth century AD and found in 1868, together with a hoard of other church metalwork and a bronze pin, inside a ring-fort at Ardagh in County Limerick. The vessel is built of silver with a bronze core, and its decoration of gold filigree, glass studs and enamel panels, executed in the interlacing animal style of Insular art, ranks it among the greatest treasures of early medieval Europe. It was probably made for use at Mass in a wealthy monastery, and it shares its technical brilliance with the contemporary Derrynaflan Chalice and the illuminated gospel manuscripts of the same age. The hoard in which it was found had been concealed in a stone-lined hollow beneath the fort, apparently during a time of danger. The chalice is displayed in the National Museum of Ireland in Dublin, where it is a centrepiece of the medieval collection and a national icon.

name: The Arrow of Arash
powers: Its single flight fixed the boundary between Iran and Turan.
description: The arrow shot by Arash the archer from the summit of Mount Damavand to fix the frontier between Iran and Turan, a flight said to have been blessed by the giving of his own strength, so that his body wasted as the arrow flew. Reaching the far bank of the Oxus at noon, the arrow ended the war between the two kingdoms and fixed the boundary for the people of Iran. The story is known from Avestan references and from Ferdowsi and other Persian sources, and the arrow's course, hundreds of miles from the Elburz peaks to the Amu Darya, has been endlessly debated and romanticised. The twentieth-century poem 'Arash the Bowmaker' by Siavash Kasrai revived the tale as a symbol of national sacrifice, and the ancient festival of Tirgan still honours the shot.

name: Aladdin's Lamp
powers: Rubbed, it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes.
description: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the oral telling of the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab and first printed around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes, while its twin, the old magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and recovery, exchanged by the sorcerer for new lamps. No medieval Arabic original of the tale survives, so the lamp is a literary invention of the folk tradition, set, like the story, in China while speaking a Syrian idiom. The image of the rubbed lamp and its wish-granting servant became one of the most widely known of all magical objects, carried into every later retelling and adaptation from pantomime to film, and its shape still means 'genie' in world popular culture.

name: The Ark of the Covenant
powers: Carried before Israel and kept in the Holy of Holies as the throne of God's presence.
description: The gilded chest built at Sinai to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, carried before the Israelites in the wilderness and kept in the Holy of Holies of the Jerusalem Temple, where it stood as the throne of God's presence. According to the biblical books it was made of acacia wood overlaid with gold, topped by a mercy seat between two cherubim, and it was borne on poles by the Levites; its presence was held to go before Israel in battle, as at the fall of Jericho. Legend holds that it was hidden away before the Babylonian destruction of the Temple, while Ethiopian tradition claims that it rests today in the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Aksum. No archaeological witness survives, so all descriptions depend on the biblical text, yet the Ark remains one of the most enduring images of sacred kingship and covenant in world culture.

name: Atlatl
material: Carved wood with antler or bone spur
powers: Hurls a dart with far greater force than an unaided arm.
description: The atlatl is the carved wooden spear-thrower that hurls darts with far greater force than an unaided arm, used across Mesoamerica from the Olmec era through the Aztec empire and beyond. Spanish accounts and Aztec codices show warriors and hunters gripping the notched end of the thrower while the dart rests in its socket, and its power is credited with punching through the cotton armour and even the mail of the Spanish at short range. The atlatl was also a ritual object: the great Aztec festivals included darts thrown in honour of the gods, and the weapon appears in the hand of deities such as Huitzilopochtli in the codices. The thrower was made of hard wood, sometimes decorated with shell and turquoise, and the socket that fits the dart's butt allowed the lever to add speed and reach. The atlatl survived in the New World long after it fell out of use elsewhere, and it is the ancestor of the spear-throwing devices of the Americas.
source: Florentine Codex and early Spanish accounts

name: Aztec Death Whistle
powers: Cuts through battle with a terrifying shriek.
description: The Aztec death whistle, sometimes called ehecachichtli or skull whistle, is a small clay whistle about three to five centimetres long, modelled as a human skull, whose internal chambers produce a shrill, wind-like and unsettling tone. The most famous examples were excavated in the late 1990s at Tlatelolco, clasped in the hands of a sacrificed man buried before a temple of the wind god Ehecatl, and they have been linked to both Ehecatl and the death god Mictlantecuhtli. Scholars such as Arnd Adje Both argue the original instruments mimicked the howling winds that Aztec souls met in the underworld rather than a human scream; the terrifying shriek heard in popular recordings comes from larger modern replicas. Whether they were blown in battle to frighten enemies is sometimes said but remains unproven, since none have been found on battlefields or in warrior graves. The whistle's grim fame has nonetheless made it a museum and internet sensation, with replicas sold worldwide.
source: Templo Mayor excavations and museum collections

name: Asson
material: Gourd rattle with snake vertebrae and beads
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Rings the spirits into the peristyle at ceremony.
description: The asson is the sacred rattle of Haitian Vodou, a gourd fitted with a handle and wrapped in a beaded net threaded with snake vertebrae, held only by the houngan or the mambo, the priest and priestess who lead the congregation. Its sound opens the ceremony: as the rattle is shaken before the peristyle, the lwa, the spirits, are called into the space, and its rhythm marks the moment they descend to possess the faithful. The beads are strung in the colors of the spirits, white for Damballah, the great serpent, black and red for Legba, yellow for Kouzen Zaka, and the gourd is kept consecrated, rubbed with red palm oil and cinnamon so that it grows dark and glossy with use. The asson is given to the priest only at the end of a long initiation, and handling another's asson is a grave offense; a related instrument, the chacha, serves the Petro rites. The rattle is thus the credential and the voice of the priest, the object that rings the spirits into the world of the living.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies

name: Amauti
material: Caribou skin with a large back hood
powers: Carries a baby in warmth against its mother's back.
description: The amauti is the woman's parka of the Inuit, cut from caribou skin with a large hood and a deep pouch across the back, the amaut, in which a baby rides warm against its mother's body. The pouch lets the child nurse and sleep without being lifted into the cold, while the hood shields mother and child together from the wind, and the whole garment is sewn with the legendary precision of Inuit women, who cut and stitch by eye so that the seams shed weather. A well-made amauti is a work of both craft and love, the fit of the pouch, the length of the tails, the fur trim at the hood's edge are all judged by the women who wear them. The garment is so central to Arctic motherhood that its making was a skill passed from mother to daughter over generations. Today the amauti is still worn in the North, and contemporary Inuit designers have carried its shape into modern fashion as a proud mark of identity.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Akan Goldweight (Abrammuo)
description: The Akan goldweight, the abrammuo, is a small cast-brass piece used from the fifteenth century onward to weigh gold dust in the trade of present-day Ghana, one of the great mercantile tools of the Atlantic world. The weights were cast by the lost-wax method, and the figurative ones depict animals, people, proverbs, objects and scenes of daily life in miniature, each one with a story to tell. The art of the weights lay in the proverb: a man could hand his companion a weight of a crocodile with a bird, and the pair would 'speak' the proverb it illustrated, making the weights a language in the marketplace. They were kept in carved boxes or purses with brass spoons and balances, and their quality was judged by law, with penalties for false weights. Collectors prize them as sculpture, but they began as everyday instruments of commerce. The goldweight joins trade, law and orature into a single small object.
source: Akan trade tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Adinkra Cloth
material: Cotton, carved calabash stamps, tree-bark dye
description: Adinkra is the stamped cloth of the Akan, dyed in dark tones and printed with the symbolic motifs that bear the same name, each one carrying a proverb and a moral lesson: the sankofa bird that looks back to learn, gye nyame, 'except God,' and dozens more that together form a written language in cloth. The dye is made from the bark of the badie tree, boiled down to a deep black, and the blocks are carved from calabash, pressed into the fabric to stamp the patterns row by row. The cloth was traditionally worn at funerals and by the bereaved, its dark ground expressing mourning while the symbols spoke of the virtues of the dead, and it is still made at the great adinkra center of Ntonso in Ghana. Today the symbols have spread far beyond the cloth, appearing in architecture, jewelry and design, but the textile remains the root of the tradition. Adinkra cloth is wisdom made wearable.

name: Agadez Cross Pendant
powers: Worn as a protective amulet, with the arms said to guard the wearer in life's directions.
description: The Agadez cross, or tanaghilt, is the best-known of the Tuareg silver pendants of Niger, a cruciform amulet with four or more arms radiating from a central square, traditionally cast by the smiths (inadan) of Agadez. Agadez and the wider Air region have their own named cross designs, and the form is sometimes said to be a stylised map, a key, or the four directions that guard the wearer on the paths of life. The pendant is given at the passages of life, at a birth, a naming, an initiation, or a marriage, and it is worn by both men and women as a protective amulet, especially in the desert, where silver is believed to bring safety and luck. Older pieces are worked in silver and niello, while modern crosses are also cast in gold for the jewellery trade. Beyond Niger, the Agadez cross has become an emblem of Tuareg culture worldwide, appearing on flags and in the tourist crafts of the Sahara even as the full meaning of the form remains a matter of oral tradition.

name: Alms Bowl Relic
description: The alms-bowl relic is the bowl that the Buddha is said to have used for his daily begging round, which became a sacred object after his death together with his tooth, his staff and other personal belongings. According to a well-known legend recorded in Gandharan art and later Buddhist texts, after the enlightenment four guardian kings, the lokapalas, each offered the Buddha a stone bowl, and the Buddha miraculously fused the four into one, so that he had a single vessel of modest size for his food. Monks of the Theravada tradition still beg with an alms bowl, holding it in both hands while householders place food in it, and the bowl is for a monk one of his few possessions, a reminder of simplicity and of the gift of the laity. In various Buddhist countries the alms bowl of the Buddha was claimed as a relic by rival pilgrim sites, and the Chinese tradition asserts that the original bowl was carried to China, where it was long venerated. For the believer the bowl embodies the Buddha's poverty and his dependence on the generous, and its veneration is part of the cult of the relics.

name: Ajrak
description: The ajrak is the block-printed shawl of Sindh, stamped in deep indigo and madder red with concentric borders of geometric stars, flowers and trellis patterns, worn over the shoulder and used to cover sacred objects. The name is linked to the Arabic word for blue, and archaeologists point to indigo-dyed and resist-printed cotton found at the Indus valley site of Mohenjo-daro as evidence that such cloth was made in the region thousands of years ago. A single ajrak may pass through some twenty-one stages of washing, printing and dyeing, using wooden blocks carved by hereditary craftsmen and mordants of iron and alum, so the finished shawl carries the redness of the earth and the blue of the river. It is a strong marker of Sindhi identity, draped at weddings, offered to guests and honoured guests, and presented as a mark of respect on formal occasions.
source: Craft history of Sindh and Sindhi cultural practice

name: Azerbaijani Carpet
description: The Azerbaijani carpet is the hand-knotted pile rug of Azerbaijan, woven on vertical looms in distinct regional schools - Karabakh, Shirvan, Tabriz, Baku, Gazakh and Ganja among them - each with its own palette, knot and field layout. The traditional repertoire of motifs includes the buta, the dragon, the medallion, the stylised garden and the khoncha offering tray, and the carpets combine rich reds, blues and ivories dyed from madder, indigo and walnut husk. Weaving was and is a women's craft, learned in the family, with the design passing from mother to daughter and the loom set up for dowry carpets that would serve the household for generations. In 2010 UNESCO inscribed the traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving on the Representative List, and the carpet remains Azerbaijan's best-known craft, displayed in national museums and in the carpet museum of Baku.
material: wool pile, cotton warp, natural dyes
era: attested from the Middle Ages; classical schools 16th-19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving' (2010)

name: Altai Komus (Jew's Harp)
description: Jew's harp of the Altai people, usually of metal or wood with a flexible tongue, played by strumming the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The komus is widely used for personal music and to accompany songs; its voice imitates natural sounds. It belongs to the same family of Siberian mouth harps as the Yakut khomus and the Buryat khuur. The player shapes the note with the mouth and breath, producing a low drone with ringing overtones that can mimic the wind, a running stream, or the calls of birds. In Altai tradition the komus was played by young men courting, by shepherds in the mountain pastures, and by singers practising the khoomei throat styles, and it is sometimes said that the sound of the komus carries the voice of the taiga itself. The instrument is small enough to be carried in the pocket, and its repertoire is largely improvised. Today the komus is performed at festivals, taught in music schools, and prized in the pan-Siberian revival of the mouth harp.
material: iron, brass or wood; steel tongue
source: ar.culture.ru 'Komus (Altai)'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections
